content:
This section of Chapter 1, "A Learnability Paradox," addresses Baker's paradox: how children converge on grammars that restrict argument structures despite receiving little reliable evidence about what is ungrammatical. Steven Pinker argues that parental feedback cannot supply the needed negative evidence. Feedback is scarce after age two, absent for verb-specific argument errors, not reliably tied to grammaticality, and noisy: twenty percent of ungrammatical utterances were repeated but so were twelve percent of grammatical ones, so treating repetition as rejection would improve the grammar a fifth of the time and worsen it an eighth (file pages 33–34). Positive evidence, by contrast, is estimated to be 99.93 percent error-free, so a learner may be better off ignoring feedback (file page 34).

Even granting probabilistic feedback, Pinker raises three further hurdles. Aggregation requires grouping "equivalent" sentences, which reopens the generalization problem; a bad-sentence verdict triggers blame assignment among many rules and among syntax, meaning, pronunciation, and pragmatics; and overt corrections demonstrably fail to change children's speech, as in the repeated "Nobody don't like me" exchange (file pages 35–36). Corrections also carry positive evidence, so any effect must be separated from that content (file page 36). Finally, negative evidence would have to be necessary, not merely helpful: uniform adult judgments about rare verbs like "I murmured John the answer" cannot plausibly rest on individual histories of correction (file page 37).

Two surrogates fail. Nonoccurrence cannot mean ruling out every unheard sentence, since infinitely many unheard sentences are grammatical; treating absence as evidence simply restates the learning problem and relocates it into the child's strategy (file pages 37–38). Uniqueness, the assumption that meanings and strings pair one-to-one, works for past tenses ("broke" rules out "breaked") but not for argument structures, because languages contain synonyms like "Give the book to me" and "Give me the book" (file pages 38–39). Discourse focus differences between datives are real but statistical and overridable by stress or clefting, making them a tenuous basis for rejection (file pages 39–40).

Strict lexical conservatism, the proposal that a verb gets an argument structure only when heard in it, is rejected for adults and children. Adults instantly accept passives or datives of rare and novel verbs ("The matrix was diagonalized," "to satellite Bob a message," "I E-mailed him the message"), while rejecting "explain" in the double-object form; denominal verbs show that lexical rules license whole sets of related structures without hearing each (file pages 40–42). Children likewise make spontaneous errors such as "Can you nut these?", evidence to be detailed in chapter 7 (file page 42).

Engineering implications, kept separate: a learning machine needs a scope-limited generalization mechanism whose permitted extensions are constrained by something other than raw absence of tokens, plus a blame-assignment procedure that attributes a rejected output to a specific rule rather than to the whole system. Innate or built-in machinery for forming equivalence classes and lexical rules is distinguished from acquired knowledge of which verbs actually take which structures; the text supports the former as a hypothesis, not as a demonstrated universal learning law. Perception, memory, time, causation, goals, analogy, creativity, emotion, and social cognition are not treated here beyond the role of perceptual context in recovering meaning. The section is text-based and legible; the printed page labels 12–21 are visible.
